content: According to tracked metrics, rail capacity reached a maximum value of 75.0 million tons in 2021 before declining to a minimum value of 65.0 million tons in 2023. Concurrently, public sources tracking disruption events indicate that these logistical interruptions peaked inversely to capacity. Disruption events reached a maximum value of 25.0 in 2023, directly aligning with the lowest recorded rail capacity of 65.0 million tons. Following this peak, disruption events showed an overall decreasing trend, falling to a minimum value of 10.0 by 2025. These metrics underscore how directly disruption events impact overall rail capacity, thereby affecting the broader coal supply chain and operational efficiency at processing plants that rely on steady inbound material flows. To contextualize these capacity and disruption trends, regional case studies provide critical insights into the operational realities of coal logistics. As of June 2026, disruptions in coal transport within Mpumalanga, South Africa, continue to be influenced by various interconnected factors, including longstanding infrastructure issues and the broader decline of coal mining in the region. When rail carriers fail to maintain strict delivery timetables due to these network impacts, toll washing operations are forced to absorb the resulting volatility, leading to inefficient labor utilization and suboptimal equipment deployment. The broader reliability of the coal supply chain is the final critical element, as it directly affects the consistency and predictability of toll washing demand cycles. Supply chain reliability is influenced not only by the physical movement of trains but also by shifting regional processing conditions and the evolving economic landscape of coal sourcing. A notable event impacting regional supply chain dynamics is the reported closure of the MERC facility in June 2026, a development that could significantly alter regional coal processing and routing strategies [86] . Despite this closure, maritime and rail logistics continue to adapt, with locations such as Monroe expected to maintain supply continuity by receiving eastern coal via vessel and Powder River Basin coal via train [86] . These shifts in sourcing routes necessitate highly adaptable rail networks. Furthermore, the economic parameters governing these supply chains have seen historical shifts that influence rail utilization.
